newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Mountbatten the man - "my cousin the king".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mountbatten the man - "my cousin the king".

text.p: Reuters assigned Doon Campbell to New Delhi in March 1947 to cover the British transfer of power to India on August 15. He looks back in the following article, written in the form of a diary, on the hectic pace in the weeks preceding India's independence
What a hysterical grind it has been in the months before India wins freedom from British rule. The last viceroy of India Lord Louis Mountbatten sets some pace.
He can be quite terrific. During a press conference the other day he referred to himself as "this chap".

Viceroys are traditionally addressed as "Your Excellency". Especially in Imperial Delhi, more royal than Buckingham Palace sometimes. But one bright member of the press got up and asked: "If India wants the British to do something or other what will 'this chap' do then?"

Mountbatten took it in good humour. He has a way of talking to his seniormost subordinates: If you don't have this done by such and such a date, you're sacked. They usually have it done before that date. And they see the twinkle in his eye.

I know not where he gets his energy. He will sit through a movie until midnight, then tackle a formidable pile of documents. He scans and digests each one at speed and is quite capable of ringing up one or other of his advisers at 2:30 a.m. and saying:
"Look, old boy, I want a map of this or a detailed report of that on my desk at 8 a.m."
The poor fellow at the receiving end, sleepy or drunk or whatever, must have ready on the dot whatever he's been asked for even if it means rousing an entire secretariat.

While Mountbatten is certainly a smoothie, he is mentally razor sharp and tremendously resourceful. He has brains -- and theatrical talent. He is an extrovert, the world's most up-market name dropper -- "my cousin the king" stuff, yet no snob and intensely human.
INDIA MUDDLED AND DIZZY BEFORE FREEDOM

People and politicians in India are a bit muddled and dizzy right now, two months before independence -- things have moved with such a rush that there is an inclination to pause and gulp for breath, to sit back and try to figure out just what is happening.
It is quite momentous. It is unlikely that India -- as a physical and geographic unit -- will disappear with its partition into India and Pakistan.

When the plan has been implemented, Congress will represent that it is not a question of two Indias but of one India with areas seceding from the centre. These areas will, of course be known as Pakistan -- a truncated, bisected country, with a lobe on either side of India.
Jinnah will need to muster all the forces, talents and resources of Moslem India to make Pakistan a going concern.

India, with its mines, minerals, mills and human masses should be a sound enough economic proposition, but few of the leaders will be content until the passage of time and the processes of circumstance prove the words uttered at an historic hour in the destiny of the land by Nehru:
"India's heart is broken, but her essential unity has not been destroyed."
With fellow journalist Mohsin Ali, I flew to Peshawar to cover the referendum in the turbulent North West Frontier Province (NWFP).
The NWFP, the Punjab, where the Sikhs wanted their own state, and Bengal looked like being Mountbatten's most troubled Provinces.
While the majority of the NWFP population was Moslem, the province was governed by allies of the Congress Party. Communal tension had erupted into violence and massacre in several areas.

Unease was growing in the mediaeval walled city of Peshawar where Pathans, often armed with home-made rifles, strutted through the narrow streets. Women wore the burka, completely covering themselves, with slits for eyes and breathing.
The Congress leader was a tribal chieftain Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan, a bearded Moses-like figure, six feet four inches tall, with craggy, defining features typifying the spirit of the Pathans.

Associate of Nehru and Gandhi in the Indian Independence struggle, the Khan, the "Frontier Gandhi" started campaigning against the British in 1920. After the British he fought the Pakistanis. They both jailed him.

We were welcomed with large baskets of fruit in our Green's Hotel rooms. Peshawar's picturesque bazaar was replenished regularly by camel caravans from Kabul with skins, wool, fruit, crockery, watches and weapons. Restaurants offered the best kebabs I'd ever tasted. And genuine VAT69.

We hired a car and headed for the Khyber, a brooding god-forsaken pass, through barren forbidding hills. Along the 12-mile route into the heart of the Pathan kingdom we passed many tribesmen, all with rifles.

Mohsin conversed in Pushtu or Urdu with one local leader offering hospitality. On the return drive we tasted it: I could hardly swallow much less digest the half-roasted sheep killed while we were on the way to Charbagh to look into Afghanistan.

We saw weapons being made, a thriving cottage industry in arms where every imaginable sort of gun -- shotgun, rifle, revolver, and you name it, others of sophisticated design -- was being expertly fashioned by a man squatting on an earthen floor in a cave.

In this country state, laws seldom extended beyond the highway. Off the road in walled villages and on mountain tracks, tribal elders administered their own laws. Among Pathan tribesmen the blood feud and the vendetta were an integral part of existence.
The tribesmen, some of the toughest warriors in the world now looking gnarled and wizened with age, eyed us warily.

Reminders of the Khyber's historical importance as a military route to the plains of India remained -- the picket posts on the hilltops and forts where advance parties would spy out the way ahead before a British regiment marched past.
